appraisal_events.evidence: 'C'est quelqu'un de très mal... De très, très mal,' Mme de Villeparisis says of Borodino, blamed by Robert's family for granting the leave that enabled his 'liaison infâme'; she mocks his title with ironic emphasis ('le Prince de Borodino, en femme pour qui l'Empire ne compte pas'), then ends in a private, knowing smile at the narrator.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme de Villeparisis voices Robert's family's anger at Borodino for enabling the affair and dismisses his Napoleonic princely title as beneath old-aristocratic notice, though the narrator frames her virtuous indignation as characteristically ironic for a Guermantes and shows it dissolving into a private smile, softening its force.

appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch praises Saint-Loup's good breeding via an anecdote about a casual introduction to a young man later revealed to be the son of Sir Rufus Israël, whom Bloch's family regards as near-royal but whom the Guermantes world sees as a tolerated foreign parvenu, so the story lands as incomprehensible to those present; the narrator also notes Bloch's own remarks are themselves badly mannered without his realizing it, and that his enthusiasm for the wealthy intermediary who told him the story has 'l'accent d'enthousiasme qu'on n'apporte qu'aux convictions qu'on ne s'est pas formées soi-même.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Bloch's social misjudgment — his own poor manners contradicting the very praise he is offering, and his mistaken belief that Sir Rufus Israël commands real prestige in the aristocratic world — while the same anecdote independently affirms Saint-Loup's genuine, unaffected courtesy.

status_effects.explanation: Openly called 'very, very bad' and blamed by Robert's family for enabling the affair.
His princely title is pointedly mocked as Napoleonic and illegitimate by Mme de Villeparisis, a witnessed put-down of his rank within the old-aristocratic value system.
His own poor manners and misjudgment of real social hierarchies are exposed even as he praises good breeding in others.
Independently affirmed, through Bloch's own account as endorsed by the narrator, as genuinely simple and well-mannered, unaffected by the young man's wealth.

ambiguities: Sir Rufus Israël's social standing is read oppositely by Bloch's family (near-royal) and by the Guermantes milieu (a tolerated foreign parvenu); this clash is central to why Bloch's anecdote falls flat, but no direct status effect is recorded for Rufus Israël himself since he is not a scene participant.
